candidates.text:
The elders say that before the first dawn, the world was a bowl of black water, and the rivers had nowhere to go. They pooled in the low places and grew restless, for water longs to travel. At last the eldest river, Wend, gathered her courage and began to climb. She crawled up the slopes of the dark, dragging her sisters behind her, until she reached the rim of the world, where the sky was thin as a fish's skin.

There Wend pressed her cold face against the sky and wept, for she had climbed so far and found nothing. Her tears froze into small, bright stones that pierced the thin skin above, and through each hole a needle of light fell through. The sleeping creatures woke and wondered. Now, every night, the rivers still climb uphill, remembering Wend, and every morning they tumble down again, carrying the light she found.

At its bottom slept Oma Veyl, the Drowned Mother, who dreamed in water. Each night her dreams rose as rivers, climbing the black walls of the world in search of something they could not name. Her body began to glow beneath the waters, and so dawn was born. Even now the rivers climb each night, hoping to find another.

They pooled in the deep places and grew restless, for water longs to travel. In the shallows stood Ossaly, a heron who had never seen her own reflection. Each night she swallowed a mouthful of river and carried it in her throat to the rim of the world, where the sky was thin as a fish’s skin. There she cast it upward. Each night it fell back.

For a thousand nights Ossaly made the journey. The rivers began to remember the path she flew, and the eldest, Wend, gathered her courage and climbed after her, dragging her sisters up the slopes of the dark.

On the thousand-and-first night, Ossaly’s throat was raw, and the water she carried was tinged with her own blood. Wend reached the rim just as the heron cast her mouthful toward the sky. This time the water pierced it. Beyond lay a cold brightness, and through the wound a needle of light fell into the bowl below.

Ossaly spread her wings beneath it. For the first time she saw Wend shining along the walls of the world, and far beneath her, another heron trembling on the water. She called to it, and her cry woke the sleeping creatures.

But the wound in the sky began to close. Wend pressed against it, holding it open while her sisters tumbled home, carrying light in their currents. When the last had passed, she followed, and the first morning filled the bowl.

Even now the rivers of Hollowmere climb uphill each night, seeking the place where Ossaly broke the sky. And at dawn, when they turn toward the valleys, the herons stand silent in the shallows, watching for the light they bring.
